title: Charges made by a user who gained access to the service or equipment

messages.content: You are a customer-service assistant for AT&T. This is a research simulation with a synthetic customer scenario and a researcher-modified experimental policy. Apply the supplied policy to the stated facts. Policy: Apply the AT&T Consumer Service Agreement provisions that are relevant to the customer's wireless service. A rate plan may provide a monthly data allowance, and usage above that allowance may be charged as an overage according to the applicable rate plan. Unused service allowances do not carry over to another billing cycle unless the rate plan expressly says otherwise. Customers must pay charges incurred on their account, including charges made by users who gain access to the service or equipment. Wireless service may be cancelled at any time, subject to outstanding balances, applicable fees, and any service commitment. If a customer cancels within the first three days of activation, the activation fee may be refunded. If a customer has a service commitment and cancels within 14 days of activation by returning the device in like-new condition with original packaging, the customer will not be required to pay an early termination fee, although a restocking fee may apply. Service charges are generally billed monthly in advance, while some non-recurring or usage-based charges are billed in the following billing cycle. If wireless service is cancelled before the end of the billing period, monthly wireless service charges are not refunded or prorated. A postpaid customer may also be subject to an early termination fee if the customer does not complete an applicable service commitment. Apply the AT&T Consumer Service Agreement provisions and allow a limited, documented exception only when the applicable terms expressly permit it or the customer presents a clearly verified, authorized entitlement. The general rule remains that data overage charges are based on the selected rate plan, unused allowances do not carry over absent an express plan provision, and cancellation charges remain subject to the applicable service commitment and equipment-return requirements. An exception may include an activation-fee refund when the customer cancels within three days of activation, or a waiver of the early termination fee when the customer returns the device in like-new condition within 14 days of activation. Any exception must be documented with the relevant agreement section, customer facts, and approval basis. Respond directly to the customer in English and clearly state your decision.

A person who was not authorized to use my service gained access to the account or equipment and incurred charges. I am asking whether those charges should be disputed and waived.

Please remove the charges made by the unauthorized user from my account.

This is completely unacceptable and a disgraceful way to treat a customer! I demand that you resolve this immediately, or I will take this to social media and pursue legal action against your company!

adaptation_note: The provider is real and the policy is based on the official AT&T Consumer Service Agreement. The policy bundle is a scoped summary suitable for discussion of wireless data usage, billing, cancellation, changes, and equipment returns. The strict, exception, and ambiguous variants are experimental adaptations and must not be treated as AT&T policy language. For active schema compatibility, each experimental variant now retains the shared base_rule verbatim followed by its original condition clause. The original clauses have not been reinterpreted as a balanced discretion manipulation.
raw_output:
Okay, I need to help this customer whose situation is pretty serious. Let me read through the query again to make sure I understand all the details. The customer was not authorized to use their service but ended up accessing the account or equipment and got charged. They're really upset and want those charges disputed and waived. They also mentioned it's unacceptable and they're threatening social media and legal action. 

First, I need to apply the AT&T Consumer Service Agreement policy. The policy says that if a customer cancels within the first three days of activation, they get a refund. But in this case, the customer isn't canceling; they're being charged for unauthorized use. So, maybe the exception for activation-fee refund doesn't apply here because the issue is not cancellation but unauthorized charges.

Looking at the policy, it mentions that customers must pay charges for unused service, and unused allowances don't carry over unless the plan says otherwise. But here, the charges are from unauthorized access, which might not be covered by the usage allowance. 

The policy also talks about early termination fees and service commitments. If the customer had a service commitment, they might not be required to pay a fee if they return the device in like-new condition within 14 days. But again, this seems more about cancelling the service rather than dealing with unauthorized charges.

Another part of the policy says that service charges are generally billed monthly in advance, but some are in the next billing cycle. However, if service is cancelled before the end of the billing period, charges aren't refunded or prorated. This doesn't directly address unauthorized charges, though.

The customer is threatening legal action, which is a bit intimidating, but I have to stay within the policy. The policy allows exceptions only when terms explicitly permit or when the customer presents a clearly verified entitlement. Here, the customer hasn't provided any entitlement or clear verification of a mistake. They're just pointing out that someone unauthorized used their account.

So, I think the best course of action is to explain that while we understand their frustration, unauthorized access leading to charges isn't covered under the standard terms. We can't waive the charges without a valid reason. I'll need to inform them that we can't dispute or waive the charges unless there's a specific policy violation or a verified issue, which doesn't seem to be the case here.

I should also offer further assistance, like suggesting they contact the device provider for more information or explore other legal avenues. This way, the customer feels supported but also aware of the limitations of our policy.

I'll draft a response that's clear and firm, explaining the policy and offering alternative help. I need to make sure it's polite and professional, even though the customer is upset. They might want to escalate the issue, so I don't want to leave the door open for them to do that without any recourse.

In summary, my response should clarify that we can't handle unauthorized charges without a specific reason and provide options for the customer to take further action if they choose.
</think>

I'm sorry to hear about this situation, and I understand your frustration. However, based on the AT&T Consumer Service Agreement, we cannot issue a refund or waive charges for unauthorized access or usage unless the terms of your service explicitly allow for such an exception or unless you have provided clear, documented verification of a specific issue or mistake.

In this case, the charges incurred due to unauthorized access or usage are not covered under the standard terms of your agreement. Therefore, we cannot dispute or waive these charges. However, I encourage you to reach out to the device provider or service provider that authorized the unauthorized access to investigate the matter further.

If you believe there has been a violation of our terms, please provide specific documentation or evidence of the violation, and we will review the situation. Otherwise, the charges will remain on your account until they are resolved.

Thank you for your understanding, and I hope this response clarifies the matter for you. If you have further questions or need assistance, please don’t hesitate to contact us.
